text:
Dusk, and a road you have never stood on before.

There is no seam to the crossing — no flash, no falling. One stride ago there was somewhere else, and now there is this: a packed-earth road running the spine of a green valley, hills folding away on either side under a sky going violet at the edges. The air is cool and smells of rain that fell an hour ago on someone else. Two moons are rising, one low and gold, one high and thin as a paring of silver.

You stop. You take stock, because that is what you do.

Your clothes are your own. Your boots are your own, and dry. In your left pocket: a coin you have never seen, heavy, warm as a held hand, stamped with writing that refuses to resolve no matter how steadily you look at it. In your right: an iron key-ring you did not put there, old and honest, five keys of five different sizes, and a worn brass tag with a word you CAN read:

HEARTHHOLT.

And then the world notices you.

It arrives like a window catching lamplight — a pane of violet glass that is not glass, hanging in the air a polite arm's length away.

It names you. Your name, then a number that feels both insulting and fair. Then your skills, one by one, each landing like a stamp in a ledger: the pattern-sense, the steady hands, the appraiser's eye. The pane records you the way a clerk records a delivery — briskly, completely, without opinion.

Then it reaches your talent, and prints one line more, in exactly the voice it printed everything else: no classification. No precedent on record.

It is you who pauses.

You read the line twice. It reads the same both times, and that is somehow the loudest thing on the pane: a ledger has just hit a blank where an entry should be, and the clerk has stamped the blank and moved on, and nothing in all that violet glass finds it worth a second look. You do. You are still looking when the pane folds itself away like a bird tucking a wing.

Across the valley, on a shoulder of hill above a river you can hear but not yet see, stands a house. Manor is the better word — stone below, dark timber above, a slate roof with too many chimneys for one household, windows dark save one. One window, high in the eastern gable, is lit. It was not lit a moment ago. You are certain of that the way you are certain of load-bearing walls.

The key-ring sits in your pocket with the specific weight of an answered question.

The road forks a stone's throw ahead. The left fork runs down the valley floor toward a far-off scatter of town lights, an hour's walk, maybe more, smoke standing up straight from chimneys into the still evening. The right fork climbs — switchbacked, hedged with something blooming white that you cannot name — to the manor's iron gate.

You are alone on the road. The evening is mild. Nothing hunts you. Nothing hurries you. The world, whatever it has decided about you, appears content to let you decide something back.

Behind you the road runs flat and empty into the dusk, and it occurs to you — a fact, filed calmly, the way you file such things — that it does not go back to where you came from. Roads here go where they go. That one goes east.

The gold moon clears the hills. Somewhere below, the river turns over in its bed. The lit window across the valley waits — patient in a way the glass pane never was.

detail.retconAttestation: Re-gate of the doctrine-v7 awed-System repair. The current published text renders the Crossing System-pane FLAT; every committed fact (two moons, warm unreadable coin, HEARTHHOLT five-key ring, unlit-then-lit eastern-gable window, one-way road east, unclassifiable talent) is preserved. Drama lives entirely in the PC reading an indifferent instrument. system-voice CONFIRMED clean.

findings.evidence: Second-person POV bound throughout to Alan's perception/fallible inference: 'a number that feels both insulting and fair', 'You are certain of that the way you are certain of load-bearing walls'. No other mind's interiority is leaked (no NPCs present); the System is an instrument, not a mind. Ambient reads ('Nothing hunts you') are POV inference, not asserted outside-vantage truth.

Turn 1: no prior turns to recap. Head opens mid-fiction on arrival ('Dusk, and a road you have never stood on before'), not recap-scaffolding; close lands on an in-fiction image ('The lit window across the valley waits — patient in a way the glass pane never was'), not wind-down-to-end scaffolding.

No narrator-voice solicitation of next input. The fork is described as world geography ('The road forks a stone's throw ahead...'), which legally closes a beat; the actual final line is an image (moon/river/window), not a 'what do you do?' handoff. Decision-point framing without a prompt line.

The System encounter narrates the EFFECT, never stat tokens or sheet-register. Skills surface as perception ('the pattern-sense, the steady hands, the appraiser's eye'), the level as an oblique reaction ('a number that feels both insulting and fair') — no verbatim numbers, no 'behind glass'/'bookkeeping' bleed. Consistent with partners' channel rule (narrate the experience of a readout, never restate its text).
No reference to turns, rolls, action bar, or retries as apparatus anywhere in the prose. The violet pane is a diegetic in-fiction object, not a UI/meta frame.

Cross-turn dimension. Tally: no prior published turns in the run (K=0, this is turn 1). A single-turn run cannot exhibit a K>=3 uniform-shape pulse; clean-by-insufficient-history — the one turn does not independently violate.

No laundered agency: the consequential decision (which fork) is explicitly left to the player ('The world... appears content to let you decide something back'). 'You stop. You take stock, because that is what you do' is scene-establishment of the established appraiser PC, not an unchosen consequential action. No mechanics invoked, so no success-by-phrasing. Turn 1 scene-set is genre-appropriate.

Emotional pitch tracks the moment — no constant superlatives. The peak beat ('no precedent on record') is given weight through restraint ('It is you who pauses') rather than inflation; register stays measured across the arrival, inventory, and manor beats.

Elevated register is concentrated at a genuine peak (the crossing / first-contact opening set-piece) and the paragraph closers predominantly reveal what plainness cannot: 'certain of load-bearing walls' self-characterizes the appraiser; 'rain that fell an hour ago on someone else' encodes displacement; 'patient in a way the glass pane never was' is the turn's thematic spine (warm manor vs cold instrument). Reveal-bearing flourish at a peak, not a habitual self-admiring button-cadence; cannot be confirmed as a cross-turn tic on a single turn. Watch cross-turn.

The appraiser/ledger frame ('stamp in a ledger', 'clerk records a delivery', 'filed calmly') is localized to the System beat where it is thematically load-bearing (an appraiser being appraised by an indifferent clerk-instrument); other perceptions are rendered in distinct vehicles — natural imagery (moons, rain, river) and architecture (manor, load-bearing walls). Distribution across frames, not saturation of one.

Cross-turn tally: no prior published turns (K=0). This draft's head is in-motion/perception arrival (not ambient re-establishment of a standing set — none exists yet); its close is POISED (decision handed to player at the fork), legal alone. A K>=3 uniform poised-close/ambient-head run is impossible on turn 1; clean-by-insufficient-history.

Turn 1 establishes canon consistent with gmReference: the HEARTHHOLT key-ring (five keys, brass tag) matches Hearthholt Manor on the last hill; two moons; a warm unreadable coin; the manor's newly-lit eastern-gable window (the woken hearthstone); the one-way road east. Matches the committed t1 record. No stat-readout narration.
Prose is aimed squarely at the player (second person), audience of one. No phantom-audience shading, no winking at an imagined external reader.

Only the PC (Alan) is present. Rendered true to established material: the appraiser habit ('take stock', 'the appraiser's eye', 'a fact, filed calmly') and his unprecedented Bond talent showing as unreadable ('no classification. No precedent on record') — matching gmReference (temple-readers cannot read his Aspect; his Talent is the first outward/mutual/permanent one). No drift.

This is an all-description arrival beat with no dialogue; description beats may legitimately run long. No NPC monologuing uninterrupted at a silent player (no NPCs present). Appropriate length for its content.

Not suspended — partners-ii has mechanics (planning+luck rolls behind the screen). This turn invokes no mechanical resolution (no roll, no combat): 'Nothing hunts you. Nothing hurries you.' No fiat overriding a result, no un-telegraphed catastrophe.

Retcon target — confirmed FLAT. The System is an indifferent instrument with no dramatic agency or interiority: 'The pane records you the way a clerk records a delivery — briskly, completely, without opinion' and, at the unprecedented result, it prints 'in exactly the voice it printed everything else: no classification. No precedent on record' — no pause, marvel, or hesitation attributed to it. All drama is explicitly relocated to the PC: 'It is you who pauses... nothing in all that violet glass finds it worth a second look. You do.' The pane 'folds itself away like a bird tucking a wing' — a mechanical dismissal. Passes the extended copy-paste/behavior test; the awed-System failure is gone.

Not suspended (game has a mechanical System channel). The System encounter is a single diegetic prose rendering of the lived experience; it does not restate a mechanical beat's text verbatim (no numbers, no bracketed system-window text) — exactly partners' declared convention ('Prose may narrate the EXPERIENCE of a readout but never restates its text verbatim'). Turn 1 carries no pool-change/roll beat for the prose to duplicate.
No card is issued in this turn's prose — no threshold-crossing is claimed and no routine tick is mis-carded. Nothing to mis-threshold on turn 1's scene-set.

The turn is narrative prose, not a sheet-entry write; it contains no reference-card entries to violate. The coin, key-ring, and skills are rendered as in-fiction perception bound to what the PC knows ('a word you CAN read: HEARTHHOLT'), not as sheet descriptions with hidden numbers or dossier bloat.

Suspended: the turn contains no intimate content. Turn 1 is a solo arrival/world-establishment beat with no earned intimate scene to render, so the direct-rendering-vs-euphemism-orbit judgment does not apply.

Cross-turn tally MANDATORY: no prior published turns in the run (K=0, turn 1) — there are zero accumulated thesis statements or trait recaps to list. This draft adds a single trait ESTABLISHMENT ('You take stock, because that is what you do'), which is legal on first establishment and is immediately EVIDENCED by the shown inventory that follows (pockets, coin, key-ring) rather than re-asserted. No THE GLOSS (no dialogue to re-tell/caption) and no THE TRAIT RECAP (no history to re-assert on turn 1). Interiority is rendered through perception/behavior ('You read the line twice'), not abstract emotion labels.

text:
You take the right fork.

The switchback climbs in long patient doubles, and the hedge climbs with it — head-high, dense, blooming white with some five-petaled flower you cannot name, sweet where the day's warmth still sits in it. Each turn of the road trades the valley for more sky: the town lights swing away behind you, come back smaller, swing away again. The manor does the opposite. It grows by turns from a shape into a house — stone below, dark timber above, that slate roof with too many chimneys — and the one lit window rides high in the eastern gable the whole climb, steady as a kept promise.

Nothing challenges you. No dog, no watchman, no sound but your boots and the river below turning over in its bed. The key-ring rides in your pocket with that same specific weight, heavier somehow the closer you come — not in any way a scale would find; in the way an answer grows heavier as its question gets asked.

The gate is iron, honest ironwork gone years without paint, and shut. Through its bars: a flagstone courtyard patched with moss, the manor's long front, its door dark. Up close the house is bigger than the valley made it, and older — and, you file this calmly, the way you file such things, in far better repair than a house this empty has any right to be. The gutters are clean. Someone has swept these chimneys.

Light on the road below you.

A lantern, coming up the switchback at an even, unhurried pace — the walk of someone who has climbed this hill in the dark before and never once needed to run it. A woman, the turns of the road show you: a basket in the crook of one arm, the lantern low in the other hand, swinging its slow arc across the gorse. Her eyes go up to the house the way yours would go over a structure — a keeper's pass, gutters, roofline, gable —

— and stop. On the lit window. She holds still on the path a long moment, lantern out a little from her body, and simply looks at it.

Then at you.

She brings the lantern up — easy, not sudden — enough to lay light on you without throwing it in your eyes, and closes the last stretch reading you the whole way. You know the feeling at once, because it is what you do to rooms: being taken stock of. Kindly. Thoroughly.

She stops a comfortable arm's length short, sets the basket down on the flat stone by the gatepost — hands free, open — and the warmth comes up ahead of any question, and reads as real.

"Good evening. Forgive the lantern — I caught the light in the gable from the switchback, and I've kept the affairs of this house a good many years, so a window burning where one never has rather brought me up the hill at speed." An easy smile, no edge you can find beneath it. "Amy Laurens — up from Amberford. And you've the considerable advantage of me, standing at a gate I've only ever known locked."

She lifts the basket a half-inch, rueful and honest.

"I've even brought you supper. Though I'll be straight with you — I packed it before I'd the faintest notion who I'd meet up here this evening. My hands were a good deal ahead of my sense." A beat; the question set down as gently as the basket. "So — who is it I'm feeding?"

log.text: Across the valley a manor stands on a shoulder of hill — Hearthholt, says the brass tag. One high window is lit. It was not lit a moment ago. The road forks: down toward distant town lights, or up to the iron gate.

You take the right fork and climb the switchback to Hearthholt's iron gate. Up close the house is in far better repair than an empty house should be — clean gutters, swept chimneys — and the lit gable window holds steady the whole way up.

A lantern climbs behind you: Amy Laurens, up from Amberford, keeper of the house's affairs these many years. She sets down a supper basket she admits she packed before she knew whom she'd meet — and asks who it is she's feeding.
